The files hold the tool definitions each server served, every recorded change field by field, pattern scan matches, and advisory classifier readings. A signed manifest lists checksums so users can verify files, and the data is released under CC BY 4.0. ## What it does The site says HISTOR reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry each day and runs each new npm and PyPI MCP package version in a sandbox. It presents its pattern matches and classifier flags as leads worth reading, not as proof that a server is malicious. ### Stated on the product site License CC BY 4.0 Release cadence A full snapshot published as files once a month Verification A manifest of file checksums, signed with Ed25519 Mirrors Hugging Face with one tag per snapshot, Zenodo with a DOI per snapshot Coverage limit Servers that require a key show less or nothing to the anonymous client Code link The page links a GitHub repository for the project ### Not stated on the site * The page does not name the LLM behind the advisory classifier readings. * The page does not say what the sandbox run of a package records beyond its tool list. * How server operators' opt-out requests are handled beyond opening an issue is not described on the page. Compare the latest saved entries for one MCP server and you get zero tool names in common. Compare the observations from the same evening and all 23 tool fingerprints match. We maintain HISTOR, a transparency log for the tool definitions MCP servers advertise. We wanted to see whether an independent observer could corroborate one of our observations. We picked LEGION-tlog because it publishes a timestamp and a SHA-256 fingerprint for each tool. Those fingerprints let us compare individual definitions even when the logs use different formats for their records. LEGION developer documentation ## What the two logs saw The server was `com.aiapplyd/aiapplyd`. We compared the tool name, description and input schema using LEGION’s canonicalization rule for per-tool fingerprints. All times below are UTC in 2026. HISTOR server history · LEGION server record HISTOR observation | What the comparison showed --- | --- 19 October, 21:37:07 | All 23 fingerprints matched the LEGION observation from 22:01:05, about 24 minutes later. 24 October, 18:19:21 | All 23 names switched from `aiapplyd_` to `getmattered_`. The suffixes matched the earlier names. The latest entry in our archived LEGION response still showed the October 19 observation. 31 October, 12:45:49 | HISTOR recorded a set of 40 tools. None of their names appeared in the archived LEGION record. This is the set in the November 2 HISTOR snapshot. Another team's log is how we found out ## TL;DR HISTOR, a tool reading MCP servers, stopped receiving data from 2,195 servers for three days. This failure went undetected until an overlapping log revealed the issue. The article discusses the technical causes and offers insights for MCP client development. ## Key points * HISTOR's failure went unnoticed due to high success rates in server reads, obscuring the 2,195 inactive servers. * The MCP revision changed the session initiation process, leading to compatibility issues. * A new logging tool, ScraperWatch, helped detect the problem by contrasting its findings with HISTOR's. ## Quick facts Affected Servers -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- HISTOR — transparency log for MCP tool definitions (https://alexar76.github.io/histor/) citeturn49search5 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: 5 days ago; HISTOR keeps a public, signed record of what every remote MCP server in the official registry advertised, and tells you the day it changed. ... Other logs, the same servers ## Outside checks HISTOR is not the only public record of MCP tool definitions. Where another log publishes its reads, the two are compared on the same servers and days, and the result is published both ways, with HISTOR's own misses. ### ScraperWatch A daily diff of a fixed panel of about 3,000 remote endpoints. HISTOR compares each of their published days with its own reads, and ScraperWatch shows the result on its page under "Outside check". The first comparison found a robots.txt parsing limit on their side and a handshake regression on HISTOR's; both were fixed the same day. scraperwatch.com/mcp-changes /datasets/peers/scraperwatch/latest ### heldfast An open daily record of the tool definitions of the servers in the official MCP registry. Of the 23,190 servers both logs recorded on 26 October 2026, 21,215 had every field in both; on those, 97.9% of servers and 99.1% of tools were identical byte for byte, and each difference has a stated cause: package versions, read times, failed reads, a first page only, an older protocol. github.com/rufat325/heldfast /datasets/interop-digests-2026-10-31 For clients, registries and server authors ## Use it Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received.
